nameStory: This tiny beetle earned the 'flea' part of its name from its impressive jumping ability — when disturbed, it can spring away like a miniature flea! The 'plantain' refers to its favorite food, the broad-leafed plantain weeds that grow in disturbed soils, while 'northern' distinguishes it from its southern relatives.
description: The Northern Plantain Flea Beetle is a tiny, shiny beetle about the size of a pinhead that specializes in munching on plantain plants. These small, dark-colored beetles have enlarged hind legs that give them their characteristic jumping ability. You'll typically see them as small, moving dots on plantain leaves, often creating distinctive small holes as they feed. Despite their diminutive size, they can be quite numerous on their preferred host plants.

idTips.label: Jumping behavior
idTips.description: When you approach or gently touch the plant, these beetles suddenly disappear with a quick hop — their enlarged hind legs launch them away like tiny springs

idTips.label: Size and color
idTips.description: About 2-3mm long (smaller than your pinky nail), with a dark metallic sheen that can appear black, bronze, or greenish depending on the light

idTips.label: Feeding damage
idTips.description: Look for small, round holes in plantain leaves — the damage looks like someone used a tiny hole punch on the foliage

idTips.label: Host plant association
idTips.description: Almost always found on broad-leaved plantain (the common 'weed' with ribbed, oval leaves), rarely straying to other plants

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Oval and slightly domed like a tiny football, with a smooth, hard shell that feels slick to the touch if you can catch one

habitat: Look for these beetles anywhere plantain grows — disturbed soils, lawn edges, roadsides, vacant lots, and garden borders throughout New England. They thrive in areas with compacted soil where plantain thrives, from sea level to moderate elevations. You'll find them most readily in sunny to partially shaded spots where their host plants are established.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge and begin feeding on young plantain growth. This is when they're most active and easiest to spot on fresh foliage.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with multiple generations possible. Look for both adults and their feeding damage on mature plantain plants.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue feeding into early fall, preparing for winter. Activity slows as temperatures drop but they remain visible on warm days.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in soil debris and leaf litter near their host plants. Not visible or active during cold months.

funFact: These beetles can jump up to 100 times their own body length when startled — equivalent to a human jumping over two football fields in a single bound!
confusionNotes: Other small flea beetles jump too, but most feed on different plants like cabbage family crops or nightshades. If it's jumping off a plantain plant, you've likely found the right species — plantain flea beetles are very host-specific.
contextualKnowledge: Many gardeners consider both the beetle and its host plant (plantain) to be unwanted visitors, but plantain is actually an edible wild green that some call 'nature's bandaid' for its traditional medicinal uses.
compareHints: Since this is the only Dibolia species in our dataset for New England, compare it to other flea beetles in the leaf beetle family. Unlike crucifer flea beetles that prefer cabbage-family plants, or potato flea beetles on nightshades, the Northern Plantain Flea Beetle is remarkably faithful to plantain. It's also generally darker and smaller than many of its crop-pest relatives.
